title: Enterprise failure injection and resilience runbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Summary
-------
This runbook describes a safe, repeatable program for conducting failure-injection and resilience validation exercises for enterprise tenants that use Redwood Inference (hosted, Dedicated, or Private). The goal is to validate customer-facing behaviours (failover, throttling, model fallback, and data isolation) and ensure Customer Success (CS) and Support teams have playbooks for communication, rollback, and remediation.

Scope
-----
- Applies to enterprise onboarding, stability game-days, and periodic resilience testing for dedicated/private tenants.
- Exercises include network partitioning, ingress throttling, model variant fallback, KV cache eviction, GPU preemption simulation, and telemetry loss scenarios.
- Not intended for experiments that modify persistent customer data or escalate to legal/regulatory gates without prior approvals.

Goals and acceptance criteria
----------------------------
- Assert that customer SLOs degrade gracefully with automated fallback policies engaged (latency SLO: p95 < 750ms under nominal; during controlled degradation, p95 may increase to 2s but requests must not return internal server error > 1% for 1h).
- Validate canary rollback path: 100% automated switchback to last-known-good model or region within 5 minutes of abort.
- Telemetry completeness: 99% of experiment events are recorded and grouped under experiment_id tag within Redwood tracing/metrics.
- Customer-facing incidents are handled within the escalation SLA documented in the Customer Incident Communications Matrix.

Owners and roles
----------------
- Experiment owner: Customer Success (CS) Solutions Engineer (primary contact for customer).
- Run executor: Platform Reliability (or customer SRE for Private installs).
- Observability lead: Observability engineer assigned to the tenant.
- Escalation liaison: Support Tier 2 lead.
- Approval authority: Customer Success manager + Security reviewer for Private/Dedicated customers.

When to use this runbook
------------------------
1. During enterprise onboarding (week 2–6) to validate cutover safety nets.
2. Prior to production model changes where rollback risk must be validated.
3. As part of quarterly resilience game-days or after major infra updates.
4. Whenever a customer requests a proof-of-resilience report for compliance.

Prerequisites
-------------
- Experiment plan approved (signed by CS manager and customer SRE if Private).
- Maintenance window scheduled and customer opt-in obtained when required.
- Backup/abort hooks verified (model pinning, routing policy override, traffic split control).
- Observability asserts configured: synthetic journey, per-route p50/p95/p99, error-rate alerts, and experiment_id tagging.
- Safety guardrails enabled: automatic circuit-breaker with threshold and manual abort endpoint.

Experiment catalogue (examples)
-------------------------------
Each experiment below includes intent, expected customer impact, telemetry assertions, and safe abort steps.

1) Ingress throttling (controlled egress saturation)
- Intent: validate adaptive rate limiter and quota-protector webhook under client surge.
- Customer impact: elevated latency, some client 429s expected within quota design.
- Telemetry asserts: 95th-percentile latency and 429-rate should match modelled profile.
- Abort: revert rate limiter to baseline policy, clear client token bucket; traffic should normalize within 60s.

2) Regional failover simulation (control-plane switch)
- Intent: ensure request routing falls back to alternate region or model variant without exposing token leakage.
- Customer impact: ~100–300ms added latency for routed requests, no data exposure.
- Telemetry asserts: requests routed via fallback path include header X-Redwood-Fallback: true and trace link.
- Abort: revert routing policy, trigger warm cache rebuild for primary region.

3) Model variant fallback under degraded GPU throughput
- Intent: validate automatic model switchover to quantized/fast variant when latency SLO is violated.
- Customer impact: small semantic variance in outputs; provide notice to customers during test.
- Telemetry asserts: model_variant metric should flip to fallback model id and tokenization stats logged.
- Abort: force-publish pinned model version for tenant and drain fallback nodes.

4) KV cache eviction and cold-start behavior
- Intent: emulate cache purge and validate KV cold-warm startup times and cost spike characteristics.
- Customer impact: transient cost spike and higher token latency for first requests.
- Telemetry asserts: cache-miss-rate, kv-lookup-latency, and per-token cost tags.
- Abort: warm caches using synthetic seeds and verify hit-rate > 90% within window.

5) Telemetry ingestion throttling / partial metrics loss
- Intent: test how downstream alerting and QBR metrics behave when observability sampling rate is reduced.
- Customer impact: none to user-facing systems, but internal dashboards may report degraded fidelity.
- Telemetry asserts: sampling tags and synthetic route alerts must surface to incident channel; missing spans must be flagged.
- Abort: restore sampling rate and reindex experiment traces.

Safe experiment design pattern
-----------------------------
- Start small: run experiments in a narrow tenant subset or sandboxed tenant.
- Canary stages: 1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% traffic, with explicit automated hold/pause gates between stages.
- Timebox: every stage should have a maximum duration and an automatic rollback trigger on threshold breach.
- Communication: annotate customer slack channel and incident bridge before starting.

Scheduling, communications and customer consent
---------------------------------------------
- For hosted customers: experiments requiring visible degradation must include email + console notification 72 hours before, and a maintenance window with opt-out link.
- For Dedicated/Private customers: follow the private deployment change control and require SRE signoff; schedule during agreed maintenance windows.
- Template customer notification: (1) summary of intent, (2) expected customer impact, (3) start/end time, (4) roll back criteria, (5) contact matrix.

Execution checklist (pre-flight)
-------------------------------
1. Verify feature-flag toggles and model pins are set.
2. Confirm observability asserts and experiment_id tagging in tracing.
3. Snapshot current routing and scaling policies.
4. Notify stakeholders and create incident bridge.
5. Run low-risk dry-run in sandbox.
6. Have abort playbook open and test abort endpoint.

Numbered procedure: running an ingress throttling experiment
---------------------------------------------------------
1. Create experiment run: POST /internal/experiments with body {\n   "experiment_id": "exp-<tenant>-20260610",\n   "type": "ingress-throttle",\n   "stage": "canary-1"\n}
2. Apply rate limit via adaptive-rate-limiter API:
   redwood-cli rate-limit apply --tenant <ID> --policy ex-throttle-1 --limit 100req/s
3. Verify traces: run query tracer.query("service:ingress AND experiment_id:<id>")
4. Wait 10 minutes monitoring p95 and error rate.
5. If thresholds exceeded (error-rate > 1% or p95 > 2s), call abort.
6. Abort: redwood-cli rate-limit revert --tenant <ID> --policy ex-throttle-1
7. Confirm traffic normalized and post metrics to experiment dashboard.

Telemetry assertions and SLO checks
----------------------------------
- Mandatory dashboards for every experiment: synthetic-journey, per-tenant error-rate, per-model latency, token-cost per-minute, and experiment_event_log.
- SLO guardrails to configure before start: p95 latency thresholds, error-rate ceilings, and model-fidelity signal (eval set pass-rate).
- Example PromQL checks:
  - latency_p95_tenant{tenant="<id>"} > 2.0 (trigger),
  - http_error_rate{tenant="<id>"} > 0.01 (trigger)

Abort/rollback paths and verification
------------------------------------
- Automated abort: circuit-breaker triggers will stop canary progression and run abort-hooks.
- Manual abort: support-runbook command documented below can be executed by Support Tier 2.
- Verification: confirm post-abort metrics return to baseline within the timewindow defined in the run plan.

Customer communications and incident templates
--------------------------------------------
- Short blurb for console banner: "Redwood is running a resilience validation for tenant <org>. Expected transient latency increases; contact <CS> for concerns."
- Incident postmortem summary template for customer: summary, timeline, root cause, impact, corrective actions, and compensation if SLA breached.

Post-experiment analysis and QBR deliverables
--------------------------------------------
- Deliverables: resilience report (one-pager), experiment artifacts (traces, config diffs, logs), customer-facing summary, and action items.
- QBR signals to include: mean-time-to-rollback, percentage of experiments passing acceptance, number of customer-visible degradations, and suggested mitigations (e.g., increase warm-start capacity, adjust model fallback thresholds).

Risk matrix and mitigations
--------------------------
- High risk: experiments that touch customer data pipelines or long-lived storage (require legal review). Mitigation: use synthetic data or isolated sandbox.
- Medium risk: full-tenant failover tests during business hours. Mitigation: timebox and use staged canaries.
- Low risk: observability sampling reductions. Mitigation: test in non-production first.

Appendix: CLI snippets and Kubernetes plays
-----------------------------------------
- Sample abort command (Support Tier 2):
  curl -X POST \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer $SUPPORT_TOKEN" \
    https://internal-api.redwood.local/v1/experiments/exp-<tenant>-20260610/abort

- Force model pin via API:
  redwood-cli models pin --tenant <ID> --model-id rwd-fast-quant-1 --reason "abort experiment"

- Simulate GPU preemption (dev-only):
  kubectl cordon <node> && kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data

Postmortem and RCA template
---------------------------
1. Executive summary (3 bullets)
2. Timeline of events (with timestamps in UTC)
3. Impact analysis (customers affected, duration, business impact)
4. Root cause hypothesis and evidence (traces, logs, recordings)
5. Remediation steps and owners (who will fix, timeframe)
6. Follow-up experiments and regression checks
